title: Philosophy: The Big Picture
objective: After this level you can explain what philosophy is, name its biggest questions and say how philosophers try to answer them with careful argument.
summary: Philosophy asks the most fundamental questions, which no experiment alone can settle, and answers them by building and examining arguments.

cards.headline: Can a question be too big for a laboratory?
cards.body: Is a law fair? What is a cause, really? Questions like these don’t fit in a test tube. This level is the whole subject in miniature: what philosophy asks, and how it tries to answer.

cards.headline: The questions under the questions
cards.body: Philosophy chases the deepest questions it can find: what the universe and we ourselves really are, how far human knowledge reaches, and what is truly valuable. A physicist asks what caused an event. A philosopher asks whether causation exists at all. If you’ve ever wondered whether a law is fair, you’ve already done some philosophy, no job title required.

cards.headline: No microscope for right and wrong
cards.body: You can’t settle these questions with an experiment alone. Try designing one that tests whether a society should value equality over freedom: not whether people think it should, but whether it should. So philosophy’s main tool is the argument: reasons, called premises, laid out to support a conclusion. Philosophers still use science, often as premises. But the argument is where the work happens, and anyone can check it.

cards.fact: Science used to be called “natural philosophy”.
cards.context: When a question becomes open to rigorous experiment, it tends to leave home and become its own field. That’s why most doctorates, even in chemistry, are still called Doctor of Philosophy. Philosophy keeps the questions that experiments can’t settle on their own.

cards.headline: It started in more than one place
cards.body: Philosophy doesn’t have a single birthplace. Thales in Greece, Confucius in China and the Buddha in India all lived within a few centuries of one another. This chapter visits all three traditions and asks how each first took on two big questions: what is real, and how should you live?

title: The Branches of Philosophy
objective: After this level you can name the main branches of philosophy (metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic, aesthetics and political philosophy) and the question each one asks.
summary: Metaphysics asks what exists, epistemology what we can know, ethics what is right, logic what is good reasoning, aesthetics what is beautiful, and political philosophy what makes a society just.

cards.headline: Every philosophical question has a home address.
cards.body: Does anything truly exist? Is it wrong to lie? Is this painting beautiful? Different questions live in different branches. Here’s the map.

items.label: Metaphysics
points: What sorts of things exist?
What is the world made of?

items.label: Epistemology
points: What is knowledge?
Can we trust our senses?

items.label: Ethics
points: What makes an action right or wrong?
What makes a life good?

cards.headline: A name that was an accident
cards.body: Metaphysics sounds mystical, but the name is a filing label. At least a century after Aristotle died, an editor, probably Andronicus of Rhodes, grouped some of his books as Ta meta ta phusika: “the ones after the physical ones”, meaning after his Physics. Aristotle never knew the word. The deepest-sounding branch of philosophy is named after a spot on a shelf.

cards.headline: Three more branches
cards.body: Logic studies good and bad arguments and reasoning: the very tool Level 1 said philosophy runs on. Aesthetics is the theory of beauty and, more broadly, the philosophy of art. Political philosophy begins with one question: what should a person’s relationship to society be? From there it asks what makes a society just or unjust.

cards.headline: One night, three branches
cards.body: Try the map on a single puzzle. You dream you’re flying. Does the dream world exist in any sense? That’s metaphysics. Can you be sure you’re awake right now? Epistemology. Is it fine to tell friends you really flew, to sound interesting? Ethics. One strange night, three branches, each asking its own kind of question.

title: Thought Experiments
objective: After this level you can explain how a thought experiment tests an idea by imagining a carefully built case instead of running a real one.
summary: A thought experiment imagines a carefully built case, like Galileo’s tied balls or Glaucon’s ring of invisibility, to test an idea; critics such as Kathleen Wilkes doubt how much they prove.

cards.headline: Some experiments need no lab, just a well-built “what if?”
cards.body: You can’t put justice in a test tube. So philosophers and scientists build imaginary cases instead, carefully, and see what follows.

cards.headline: Experiments in the head
cards.body: A thought experiment is a device of the imagination. Instead of running a real test, you picture a carefully built situation and reason about what would happen. Philosophers use them, and so do physicists, mathematicians and economists. The lab is your mind, and the equipment is free.

cards.headline: Galileo ties two balls together
cards.body: Aristotle’s view was that heavier things fall faster. Galileo imagined tying a heavy ball to a light one. The light ball should drag on the heavy one, so the pair falls slower. But the pair is heavier than either ball, so it should fall faster. It can’t do both. The theory contradicts itself, and not a single ball had to be dropped.

cards.headline: The ring of invisibility
cards.body: In Plato’s Republic, Glaucon tells of a shepherd, Gyges, who finds a ring that makes him invisible. He uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king and take the kingdom. Then comes the test: give one ring to a just person and one to an unjust person. Glaucon argues both would act alike, because people are just only when they can’t safely be unjust.

mascot.line: Keep this: a good thought experiment changes one thing and holds the rest still, like the ring does.

cards.headline: Built on purpose, doubted on purpose
cards.body: Notice how the ring is built: it removes one thing, the chance of being caught, and leaves everything else alone. That careful design is the whole method. It’s also the target of critics. Kathleen Wilkes argued in 1988 that thought experiments, especially wild ones about personal identity, give inconclusive and unconvincing results, and she preferred to study real cases.

title: Plato's World of Forms
objective: After this level you can explain Plato's theory that perfect, unchanging Forms, like Circle or Justice, are more real than the things we see.
summary: Plato held that eternal, unchanging Forms such as Beauty, Equality and Circle, known by thought, are more real than the changing things we see; his own Parmenides raises the Third Man objection.

cards.headline: You’ve never seen a perfect circle. So how do you know what one is?
cards.body: Every circle anyone draws falls a little short. Plato thought that small puzzle points to a whole hidden world.

cards.headline: Many circles, one Circle
cards.body: Plato drew a line between the many things we see and the one thing they have in common. Many things look beautiful; the Form of Beauty is what beauty really is, and those things are beautiful by sharing in it. Circles work the same way on a standard reading: the Form is perfectly circular, and every drawn circle or round ball falls short. Your doodles are fan art.

cards.headline: The equal sticks
cards.body: Here’s one of his arguments, from the Phaedo. Two sticks can sometimes look equal and sometimes unequal. Equality itself never looks unequal. So, Socrates argues, our knowledge of Equality can’t have come from the sticks, which fall short of it. We must be comparing them with something grasped by thought, not by the eyes.

cards.headline: More real than the real world
cards.body: That’s why Plato ranked the Forms above anything you can touch. The things you see change and fall short. The Forms, such as Beauty, Justice and Equality, are eternal and changeless, and they are known by thought, not the senses. For Plato, the world of eyes and hands is the rough draft.

cards.headline: Plato attacks his own theory
cards.body: The sharpest objection appears in Plato’s own dialogue, the Parmenides. If large things are large by sharing in the Form Large, and that Form is itself large, what do they all share? Another Form, it seems. Then another, forever. Aristotle called it the Third Man argument, and scholars still disagree about whether Plato thought it was fatal.

title: Aristotle's Four Causes
objective: After this level you can use Aristotle's four causes (material, formal, efficient and final) to explain what a bronze statue is and why it exists.
summary: Aristotle explained a bronze statue by four causes: the bronze (material), its shape (formal), the art of bronze-casting (efficient) and the finished statue everything is done for (final).

cards.headline: Ask “Why is there a statue?” and Aristotle hands you four answers.
cards.body: Not four guesses: four different kinds of “because”. A full explanation can use all four.

cards.headline: Made of what? Shaped as what?
cards.body: Aristotle held that you only know a thing when you grasp its cause, its “why”. A why-question has more than one kind of answer, so his four causes are four kinds of explanation. Take a bronze statue. The material cause answers “What is it made of?” The bronze. The formal cause answers “What is it?” Its form: the shape the melted bronze is poured into, which makes this lump a statue and not a doorstop.

mascot.line: Keep the four questions: made of what, what is it, made by what, and made for what?

cards.headline: Made by what? Made for what?
cards.body: The efficient cause answers “Where did the change come from?” Aristotle’s precise answer is the art of bronze-casting, the know-how in the sculptor. The final cause is what it’s for. A model is made, a mold prepared, the bronze melted and poured: every step is done for the sake of the finished statue.

cards.headline: Form, but not in the sky
cards.body: Remember Level 4’s Forms? Aristotle studied at Plato’s Academy, yet he rejected Forms that exist apart from things. For him, form lives in the thing itself. In a bronze sphere, the bronze and the roundness aren’t two separate things. Melt the sphere, and its roundness doesn’t float off to another world.

cards.headline: Bacon wants one cause out
cards.body: Not everyone wanted all four. In 1605, Francis Bacon argued that final causes belong to metaphysics, not physics. Saying clouds are “for” watering the earth, he complained, had held back the search for real physical causes. Physics, for Bacon, should stick to material and efficient causes: what things are made of and what moves them.

cards.headline: Aristotle's Four Causes: the big picture

Efficient: where the change came from

title: Confucius and the Good Person
objective: After this level you can explain Confucius's ideal of the junzi, the exemplary person, and his ideas of ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety).
summary: Confucius made the junzi a person of moral nobility, not noble birth, marked by ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety) done with real feeling; the Mohists attacked costly rituals.

cards.headline: Born noble, or become noble?
cards.body: In early China, the word Confucius built his ethics on first meant someone with the right parents. He helped make it mean someone with the right character.

cards.headline: The exemplary person
cards.body: Confucius (traditionally 551 to 479 BCE) comes down to us mainly through the Analects, a collection of his sayings and conversations. Its ideal is the junzi. The word originally meant “prince’s son”. Confucius helped turn it into a title of moral nobility, open to someone from any background. Early English translators wrote “gentleman”; some now prefer “exemplary person”. You can’t inherit it. You have to earn it.

cards.headline: Ren: humaneness
cards.body: The broadest Confucian virtue is ren, translated humaneness, benevolence or simply goodness. The same shift happened here. Before Confucius, ren described the strong, handsome look of an aristocrat. In the Analects it’s a moral excellence anyone can reach, summed up once as “caring for others”.

cards.headline: Li: ritual with feeling
cards.body: Asked about ren, Confucius spoke of overcoming yourself and returning to li, ritual propriety: the rites and etiquette of life, down to what to wear. But he had no patience for empty form. He said he couldn’t bear ritual without reverence, or mourning without grief. At a funeral, the mourners’ distress matters more than the formalities. Li is kindness that shows up on time and dressed properly.

cards.headline: The Mohist complaint
cards.body: Not everyone agreed. The Mohists, followers of the thinker Mozi, attacked the lavish funerals and long mourning the Confucians promoted. Their argument: such customs bring poverty, fewer people and disorder, so a truly benevolent person would cut them back. Both sides claimed to be the ones really caring for others.

title: Laozi and the Way
objective: After this level you can explain the Dao of Laozi and Zhuangzi and the idea of wu wei, acting without forcing, using their image of water.
summary: The Daodejing, credited to Laozi, teaches the Dao (the Way) and wu wei, acting without forcing, modelled on water; Zhuangzi’s Butcher Ding shows it, and Confucians such as Xunzi objected.

cards.headline: Nothing is softer than water. Nothing beats it against the hard.
cards.body: That riddle comes from the Daodejing, and it holds a whole philosophy of how to act.

cards.headline: The Way
cards.body: The Daodejing is credited to Laozi, the “Old Master”, said to have lived in the 6th century BCE, though some modern scholars think he never existed. Its subject is the Dao, “the way”; the character suggests a path. Its first line, in James Legge’s translation: “The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao.” Pin it down, and you’ve already missed it.

cards.headline: Be like water
cards.body: The Daodejing’s ideal of action is wu wei, often translated “non-action”. It doesn’t mean lying on the sofa. It means acting without forcing, free of grasping, self-serving desire. The model is water. It benefits everything without striving, settles in the low places people dislike, and yet nothing beats it at wearing down the hard and strong.

cards.headline: The cook who never forced it
cards.body: Zhuangzi, a later Daoist of the 300s BCE, told of Butcher Ding carving oxen. Ding doesn’t hack. He steers his blade through the natural gaps between the joints. A good cook changes knives every year; a mediocre one, every month. Ding’s knife is 19 years old and still as sharp as new. That’s wu wei with a cleaver.

cards.headline: Rivals across the table
cards.body: Daoists aimed some of this at the Confucians. Remember li from Level 6? The Daodejing says ritual propriety appears only once the Way is lost, and calls it the beginning of disorder. Confucians pushed back. Xunzi complained that Zhuangzi valued nature so highly that he failed to see the value of what is human.

title: The Buddha's Case Against a Self
objective: After this level you can explain the Buddhist no-self argument, using the monk Nagasena's chariot that is nothing over and above its parts.
summary: Buddhist philosophers argued a person is a name for five changing aggregates with no lasting self behind them, as Nagasena’s chariot shows; Nyaya critics replied that memory needs an enduring self.

cards.headline: Point to yourself. Now: which part is the self?
cards.body: Your body? Your thoughts? Your memories? A Buddhist monk once answered a king’s version of this question with a chariot.

cards.headline: A person in five parts
cards.body: The Buddha’s teaching of non-self, anatman, makes a startling philosophical claim. Look at what a person is made of: body, feelings, perceptions, volitions and consciousness, the five aggregates. Each is impermanent, always changing, so none of them can be a lasting self. And on the classical reading, there’s no extra self hiding behind them either.

cards.headline: The king’s trap
cards.body: The Questions of King Milinda stages the argument as a debate. The monk Nagasena meets King Milinda, usually identified with the Indo-Greek king Menander I. Nagasena says his own name is just a label in common use, with no permanent self behind it. The king pounces: then “Nagasena” is a mere empty sound, and you’ve spoken a falsehood!

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level, make it this: a chariot is its parts, well arranged, and nothing more.

cards.headline: The chariot
cards.body: Nagasena turns it around. You came by chariot, he says. Is the pole the chariot? The axle? The wheels? All the parts together? Something apart from them? No, says the king, every time. Then he sees it: “chariot” is the name we use for those parts put together. Exactly, says Nagasena. So is “Nagasena”. Useful name, real parts, no extra thing.

cards.headline: Who does the remembering?
cards.body: Critics weren’t persuaded. Philosophers of the Nyaya school, such as Vatsyayana and Uddyotakara, asked: if I’m a different self from yesterday’s me, how can I remember what that me experienced? Buddhist philosophers replied that causal links between events in one stream are enough, with no lasting self required.

title: India's Schools of Philosophy
objective: After this level you can name several classical Indian schools, including Nyaya, Vedanta, the materialist Carvaka and the Jains, and one idea each is known for.
summary: Nyaya built a logic of inference (smoke means fire), Advaita Vedanta identified the self with Brahman, the Carvakas trusted perception alone, and the Jains held that truth is many-sided.

cards.headline: Blind men, one elephant, and a lot of arguing.
cards.body: Classical Indian philosophers disagreed about how we know anything, what is real and what a self is. Meet four schools, with one big idea each.

cards.headline: Nyaya: where there’s smoke
cards.body: The Nyaya school, whose oldest surviving text dates to about 200 CE, made a science of knowing. It counted four means of knowledge: perception, inference, comparison and testimony. Its model inference is famous: the hill has fire, because it has smoke, and wherever there’s smoke there’s fire, as in a kitchen and unlike a lake. Yes, the proverb has a philosophy degree.

cards.headline: Advaita Vedanta: not two
cards.body: Advaita means “non-dual”. This Vedanta school, promoted by Shankara, who probably lived in the 8th century, makes a bold claim. Brahman is the fundamental reality under everything, and your individual self is, in reality, identical with it. Feeling like a separate little self is, on this view, an illusion.

cards.headline: Carvaka: seeing is believing
cards.body: The Carvakas were India’s materialists. For them, perception alone was a reliable source of knowledge; testimony and inferences about what nobody can experience didn’t count. Even consciousness, they argued, is a product of the material body. No body, no mind.

cards.headline: Jains: the many-sided truth
cards.body: Jain philosophers held that reality is many-sided, anekanta, so no single viewpoint captures the whole truth. Their famous illustration: blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant, and each describe it differently. Every report catches something, and none of them is the whole animal.

title: Checkpoint: Where Philosophy Began
objective: After this level you can compare how Greek, Chinese and Indian thinkers first asked what is real and how to live.
summary: Greek thinkers asked what is most real (Forms or form in things), Chinese thinkers how to live and govern, and Indian schools argued over the self.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: three places, two big questions.
cards.body: What is real? How should you live? Greek, Chinese and Indian thinkers gave very different first answers, and argued over the self. Line them up.

items.label: Greece
points: Plato: the most real are Forms, known by thought
Aristotle: form lives in things, like the bronze statue’s shape

items.label: China
points: Confucius: become a junzi through ren and li
Laozi: follow the Dao and act like water

items.label: India
points: Buddhists: no lasting self, only changing parts
Advaita: the self is one with Brahman

cards.headline: Rulers were listening
cards.body: Chinese philosophers spoke to rulers as well as to individuals. Training in li was part of preparing rulers and officials. Even the Daodejing gives political advice: when the sage governs through non-action, it says, good order is universal. How to live and how to rule came as a pair.

cards.headline: The self on trial
cards.body: India’s schools argued hardest about the self. Buddhist philosophers found only impermanent parts, a person named the way a chariot is. Nyaya thinkers insisted memory needs an enduring self. Advaita Vedanta went the other way entirely: your self is identical with Brahman, the reality under everything. One question, three incompatible answers, each defended with arguments.

title: Avicenna's Floating Man
objective: After this level you can explain Avicenna's floating man, a person created in midair with no sensations, and what it was meant to show about self-awareness.
summary: Avicenna’s floating man, created in midair with every sense cut off, would still be sure he exists, so Avicenna concluded the self is not the body; critics say that step doesn't follow.

cards.headline: Switch off every sense. Is anyone still home?
cards.body: No sight, no sound, not even the feel of your own arms. About a thousand years ago, the philosopher Avicenna built exactly this situation in his head, and asked what would be left.

cards.headline: A man made in midair
cards.body: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), who died in 1037, was the leading philosopher and physician of the Islamic world. In his work on the soul, he asks you to suppose a man created all at once, fully formed, with his sight veiled. He hovers in the air without even feeling it, his limbs held apart so they never touch. He has never sensed anything at all.

cards.headline: He is still sure of one thing
cards.body: Would this man affirm that he exists? Avicenna says he wouldn’t doubt it for a moment. Yet he would affirm no hand, no heart, no brain, and give his self no length, width or depth. So, Avicenna concluded, the self you are aware of is something other than the body you never noticed. Self-awareness, on this view, doesn’t come through the senses at all.

mascot.line: Keep this: knowing one thing without knowing another doesn’t prove they are two different things.

cards.headline: Two names, one man
cards.body: Scholars such as Jari Kaukua put the worry this way: the argument slides from what the man knows to what he is. You can be sure Cicero existed without being sure Tully did, though they were one man with two names. In the same way, the floating man could know his self without knowing his body, even if his self just is his body.

title: Al-Ghazali Versus Ibn Rushd
objective: After this level you can explain the debate between al-Ghazali's Incoherence of the Philosophers and Ibn Rushd's reply, including their dispute over fire burning cotton.
summary: Al-Ghazali argued that observation shows only fire and burning together, not a necessary link; Ibn Rushd replied that fire really burns and that denying causes denies knowledge.

cards.headline: Does fire really burn cotton?
cards.body: Obviously, you’d say. Hold a flame to a cotton ball and it catches. One of the most influential thinkers of Sunni Islam argued that you have never actually seen the fire do it.

cards.headline: The Incoherence of the Philosophers
cards.body: Al-Ghazali, who died in 1111, took aim at philosophers such as Avicenna in his book The Incoherence of the Philosophers. He examined twenty of their teachings. His main charge wasn’t that all of them were false, but that their arguments fell short of the strict proof the philosophers themselves demanded. His longest discussion attacks their claim that the world has always existed.

cards.headline: You only ever see them together
cards.body: His famous example: fire touches cotton, and the cotton burns. Observation, al-Ghazali argued, shows only that the burning happens together with the touch, not that it happens through it. The link isn’t necessary: you can conceive of fire touching cotton without burning it. On one account he offered, God creates the burning each time, following a habit, and the fire itself does nothing.

cards.headline: The Incoherence of the Incoherence
cards.body: The philosopher and physician Ibn Rushd of Cordoba (Averroes, 1126 to 1198) answered with a book titled The Incoherence of the Incoherence. Fire keeps its power to burn, he argued, even if something like talc can block it. Every event has four causes: agent, form, matter and end. And to deny causes is to deny knowledge, since understanding a thing means grasping its causes.

Fire and cotton: we see them together, not a necessary link

title: Maimonides and the Perplexed
objective: After this level you can explain how Maimonides's Guide for the Perplexed tried to reconcile the Hebrew Bible with Aristotle, and his idea of describing God only by what God is not.
summary: Maimonides’s Guide for the Perplexed read scripture non-literally so it could sit with Aristotle, and taught that the truest words about God say only what God is not.

cards.headline: How do you describe something that is like nothing else?
cards.body: Every word you have was made for ordinary things. In the twelfth century, Maimonides argued that the most accurate things you can say about God are the ones that say what God is not.

cards.headline: A letter to a torn student
cards.body: Moses Maimonides (1138 to 1204) was born in Cordoba and spent much of his life in Fustat, near Cairo. His Guide for the Perplexed, completed in 1190, is framed as a letter to an advanced student torn between philosophy and the teachings of his religion. Part of the cure: stop reading the Bible’s words that seem to give God a body literally, since that ends in picturing God as material.

cards.headline: Did the world have a beginning?
cards.body: Here the Bible and Aristotle seemed to clash: Aristotle’s followers held the world is eternal. Maimonides examined the arguments and concluded that neither eternity nor creation can be demonstrated. With proof unavailable on both sides, he judged creation the better-supported belief.

mascot.line: Keep this move: turn every claim into a denial. “God is powerful” becomes “God does not lack power”.

cards.headline: Say only what God is not
cards.body: Maimonides held that God is one with no parts or separate qualities, and comparable to nothing. So “God is powerful” can’t mean God has power like ours, only more. Read it as a denial instead: God does not lack power. The more you can show doesn’t apply to God, he wrote, the better. The highest praise, he concluded, is silence.

cards.headline: Too much Aristotle?
cards.body: Not everyone was grateful. The Guide was controversial, and some rabbinic circles at first banned it. Its critics asked whether its reading of the Torah really matched what the prophets meant, or owed more to Aristotle and the philosopher al-Farabi than to Moses.

title: Thomas Aquinas: Faith and Reason
objective: After this level you can explain how Thomas Aquinas combined Aristotle with Christian theology and why he held that faith and reason cannot truly conflict.
summary: Aquinas built Aristotle into Christian theology, split truths about God into those reason can reach and those only revelation gives, and blamed any clash on faulty reasoning.

cards.headline: Can faith and reason ever really fight?
cards.body: In medieval universities, students of the arts learned mostly from Aristotle. One Dominican friar set out to show that philosophy done properly could never truly clash with Christian faith.

cards.headline: Aristotle, rebuilt
cards.body: Thomas Aquinas (about 1225 to 1274), a Dominican friar who taught theology in Paris, took Aristotle as his main inspiration and built something new: a systematic reworking of Aristotle’s philosophy inside Christian theology. He wrote long commentaries on Aristotle’s works, confident that progress in philosophy could only benefit the faith.

cards.headline: Two kinds of truth about God
cards.body: Aquinas split truths about God in two. Some, such as that God exists and that there is one God, reason can reach without revelation; he called these the preambles of faith. Others, such as the Trinity, only revelation can supply. Faith takes you further than reason can go, but it never contradicts what reason knows.

cards.headline: Blame the reasoning
cards.body: So what if a philosopher reaches a conclusion that contradicts the faith? Then, Aquinas wrote, “this is not philosophy but rather an abuse of philosophy, due to a failure of reason.” Truth can’t fight truth; when they seem to, someone has argued badly. On whether the world had a beginning, like Maimonides before him, he found that no demonstration works either way.

cards.headline: What “God is good” means
cards.body: Aquinas disagreed with Maimonides on one point. Reading “God is good” as only “God is not evil” misses what people mean, he argued: saying God lives means more than that God differs from lifeless things. For Aquinas, whatever good we find in creatures exists in God first, in a higher way than we can fully grasp.

cards.headline: Condemned in Paris
cards.body: Many of his views were fiercely controversial. In 1277, three years to the day after his death, 219 propositions were condemned in Paris, a significant number of which seemed to implicate his teachings. Franciscan critics published “corrections” of his work, and his Dominican supporters fired back.

title: Wang Yangming: Knowing Is Doing
objective: After this level you can explain Wang Yangming's claim that knowledge and action are one, and the bamboo he stared at for days trying to find its principle.
summary: Wang Yangming gave up hunting for principle in bamboo, found it in the mind, and taught that true knowing already includes acting; critics reply that weakness of will is real.

cards.headline: Can you know something is wrong and do it anyway?
cards.body: Most people would say yes, all the time. The Chinese philosopher Wang Yangming said no: if you don’t act on it, you don’t yet know it. His road there began with a week of staring at bamboo.

cards.headline: Seven days of bamboo
cards.body: Wang Yangming (1472 to 1529) was a Chinese statesman, general and Neo-Confucian philosopher. As a young man he tried the method of the orthodox Neo-Confucian Zhu Xi: investigate things to grasp their principle. His friend Qian stared at the bamboos in front of a pavilion and fell ill on the third day. Wang took over and fell ill on the seventh. No principle appeared.

cards.headline: Looking in the wrong place
cards.body: Years later, in exile in what is now Guizhou, Wang had a philosophical awakening in 1508. Searching outside yourself for moral truth, he decided, had it backwards. The principle is fully present in every person’s mind. The bamboo was never going to tell him.

cards.headline: Knowing is doing
cards.body: Hence his best-known doctrine, the unity of knowing and acting. “Those who ‘know’ but do not act simply do not yet know,” he said. Being able to say something filial doesn’t mean you know filial piety. He borrowed an image from the Great Learning: hating evil is like hating a hateful odor. Recognizing the smell and recoiling from it aren’t two steps.

cards.headline: Isn’t weakness of will real?
cards.body: Picture a student caught plagiarizing who says, “I knew it was wrong, but I wanted the easy grade.” Zhu Xi, like Aristotle, would take that at face value: weakness of will. Wang would say the student didn’t really know. Critics reply that recognizing something as attractive or repellent doesn’t always lead to action.

title: Descartes Doubts Everything
objective: After this level you can explain Descartes's method of doubt, his dream and evil demon arguments, and why "I think, therefore I am" survived them.
summary: Descartes tipped out all his beliefs like apples from a basket, doubted them with dreams and a deceiver, and found one certainty: I am, I exist, whenever I think it.

cards.headline: How do you get the rotten apples out of a basket?
cards.body: René Descartes had a drastic answer, and it wasn’t really about fruit.

cards.headline: Tip out the whole basket
cards.body: Descartes compared his beliefs to a basket of apples, some of them possibly rotten. The best move is to tip them all out, then put back only the ones you can see are sound. So in his Meditations (1641) he resolved to hold back belief from anything with even some reason for doubt, hoping to reach solid ground to build on.

cards.headline: Dreams, then a deceiver
cards.body: First, dreams. You can’t be sure you aren’t dreaming right now, so your senses can’t give certainty. But awake or asleep, two and three make five. So Descartes went further and imagined a deceiver of supreme power and cunning, able to fool him even about the simplest truths.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: the Meditations never say “cogito, ergo sum”. There it’s “I am, I exist”.

cards.headline: The one thing the deceiver can’t touch
cards.body: Let the deceiver do his worst: if he is deceiving me, then I exist. “I am, I exist,” the Meditations say, is necessarily true whenever I put it forward or conceive it. The famous line “I think, therefore I am” comes from elsewhere: French in the Discourse on the Method (1637), and Latin, “cogito, ergo sum”, in the Principles of Philosophy (1644).

cards.headline: Was it overkill?
cards.body: Pierre Gassendi, one of the Meditations’ first critics, thought so. Why treat everything as false and invent a deceiving demon, he asked, when noting the weakness of the human mind would do? Descartes replied that errors soaked up since infancy don’t leave just because you say they might be there.

title: Spinoza and Leibniz
objective: After this level you can explain what made Spinoza and Leibniz rationalists, with Spinoza's "God or Nature" and Leibniz's claim that this is the best possible world.
summary: Rationalists trusted reason beyond the senses: Spinoza proved like a geometer that there is one substance, God or Nature; Leibniz argued God chose the best possible world, and Voltaire laughed.

cards.headline: Could you prove how reality works, the way you prove a triangle’s angles?
cards.body: Two 17th-century philosophers came close to trying. They trusted reason further than the senses, and reached some very bold conclusions.

cards.headline: What makes a rationalist
cards.body: Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz are traditionally grouped as the Continental Rationalists. The core claim: some of our concepts and knowledge are gained independently of sense experience, with reason supplying what the senses can’t. Historians warn the labels are rough; each thinker went his own way.

cards.headline: God, or Nature
cards.body: Baruch Spinoza (1632 to 1677) of Amsterdam built his Ethics like a geometry book: definitions and axioms first, then every proposition demonstrated from what came before. His conclusion: there is only one substance, God, and everything else is in God. Hence his phrase “God, or Nature”. That being acts from the same necessity from which it exists, not by choosing.

cards.headline: The best of all possible worlds
cards.body: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646 to 1716) started from the principle of sufficient reason: there must be a reason why things are as they are and not otherwise. Unlike Spinoza’s, his God chose one world from infinitely many possible ones. A God who is all-powerful, all-knowing and good would choose the best, so this is the best of all possible worlds.

cards.headline: Voltaire laughs
cards.body: In a world full of natural and moral horrors, that sounded absurd to many. Voltaire roundly mocked it in his novel Candide. Yet Leibniz never said everything is wonderful, only that no better world was possible as a whole.

Leibniz: God chose the best of all possible worlds
Voltaire mocked it in Candide

title: Locke, Berkeley and Hume
objective: After this level you can explain the empiricist claim that all ideas come from experience, from Locke's blank slate to Berkeley and Hume.
summary: Locke called the newborn mind a blank slate filled by experience, Berkeley said to be is to be perceived, and Hume made every idea a copy of an impression; Leibniz answered with veined marble.

cards.headline: Where did your idea of a golden mountain come from?
cards.body: You’ve never seen one, yet you can picture it instantly. David Hume said that picture is still built entirely from experience.

cards.headline: The blank slate
cards.body: John Locke’s Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) argued that we have no innate knowledge. At birth the mind is a blank slate, and all ideas, the materials of knowledge, come from experience: sensation of the world outside, and reflection on the workings of our own minds.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: Berkeley didn’t deny that apples exist. He denied they exist apart from minds.

cards.headline: To be is to be perceived
cards.body: George Berkeley went further. An apple, he said, is a collection of ideas: a colour, taste, smell, shape and firmness that go together. There’s no mind-independent matter behind them. To be is to be perceived. Critics asked whether a tree in an empty college quad stops existing; one answer Berkeley suggests is that God always perceives it.

cards.headline: Copies of impressions
cards.body: Hume split our perceptions in two: lively impressions, when we see, hear, feel or desire, and fainter ideas, which copy them. A golden mountain just joins two ideas you already had, gold and mountain. Hume even offered an exception: someone who had seen every shade of blue but one could probably imagine the missing shade.

cards.headline: Veins in the marble
cards.body: Rationalists weren’t convinced the mind starts empty. Against Locke’s blank slate, Leibniz offered a different image: a block of marble whose veins help decide which figures can be carved from it. The mind, on this view, helps determine what it can take in.

title: Kant's Revolution
objective: After this level you can explain Kant's claim that the mind shapes experience through space, time and cause, and how it answered both rationalists and empiricists.
summary: Kant argued that experience conforms to the mind, which supplies space, time and cause; that answered empiricists and rationalists, at the price of never knowing things in themselves.

cards.headline: What if you could never take your glasses off?
cards.body: Tinted lenses color everything you see, and if you’d worn them from birth you’d never notice. Kant argued that the human mind shapes experience in something like that way: space, time and cause come from us.

cards.headline: Woken by Hume
cards.body: Immanuel Kant (1724 to 1804) wrote that the remembrance of David Hume “first interrupted my dogmatic slumber”. Hume had argued that neither reason nor experience can justify beliefs such as “every event must have a cause”. Yet science and everyday life rely on them. So where do they come from?

cards.headline: Turning the question around
cards.body: In the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), Kant proposed a switch. Instead of assuming our knowledge must conform to objects, suppose objects must conform to our knowledge. He compared it to Copernicus, who made the observer move instead of the stars. The mind supplies space and time as forms of all experience, and concepts such as cause, so every event we meet has a cause.

cards.headline: Both sides were half right
cards.body: That answered both camps. Against the empiricists: the mind isn’t a blank slate; it actively structures what the senses deliver. Against the rationalists: reason alone gives no knowledge of what lies beyond possible experience. In his words, “Thoughts without content are empty; intuitions without concepts are blind.”

cards.headline: Jacobi’s complaint
cards.body: The price: we know only appearances, never things in themselves. Friedrich Jacobi spotted a strain. Kant says things in themselves affect our senses, yet by his own rules cause applies only within experience. Without things in themselves, Jacobi said, he couldn’t enter Kant’s system; with them, he couldn’t stay in it.

title: What Is Knowledge?
objective: After this level you can explain the classic definition of knowledge as justified true belief and what each of its three parts adds.
summary: Knowledge, on the classic definition, is justified true belief: it must be true, you must believe it, and you must have good support, which rules out lucky guesses.

cards.headline: You called the coin toss. Did you know?
cards.body: You said tails, and tails it was. Right answer, but was it knowledge? Most people say no. So what does knowing take, beyond being right? Here is philosophy’s most famous three-part answer.

mascot.line: Keep this: true, believed, justified. Each leg blocks a different way of being wrong about what you know.

cards.headline: A stool with three legs
cards.body: The classic definition says you know something when three things hold. It is true. You believe it. And you are justified in believing it: you have good support for it. Philosophers shorten this to JTB, justified true belief. Picture a three-legged stool. On this view, kick out any one leg and knowledge falls over.

cards.headline: Leg one: it has to be true
cards.body: Most epistemologists agree that what is false cannot be known. Eighty-four is not a prime number, so nobody could ever know that it is, however confident they feel. And truth is about how things are, not about whether anyone can prove it. A coin that nobody checks still landed one way or the other.

cards.headline: Leg two: you have to believe it
cards.body: You can only know what you believe. If you don’t believe something, you can’t know it, even if it happens to be true. That’s why philosophers call knowledge a kind of relationship with the truth: the fact has to be out there, and your mind has to hold it.

cards.headline: Leg three: good reasons, not luck
cards.body: Why add justification? Because of lucky guesses like your coin call. Plato’s Theaetetus already had the worry. Socrates points out that a skilled lawyer can talk a jury into a true belief without giving them knowledge. The jurors are right, but not because they know. Justification is the leg that keeps luck out.

cards.headline: A rival: saw off a leg
cards.body: Not everyone keeps all three legs. Crispin Sartwell argued in 1991 and 1992 that knowledge is merely true belief: if your belief is true, you know, and justification was never needed. Most epistemologists call this a heterodox view. For them, the lucky coin call is exactly why the third leg matters.

title: The Gettier Problem
objective: After this level you can explain how Edmund Gettier's 1963 cases, like the job applicant with ten coins in his pocket, show a lucky true belief falling short of knowledge.
summary: Gettier’s 1963 cases show a belief that is true, believed and justified yet true only by luck, so justified true belief is not enough for knowledge.

cards.headline: Right, careful and still wrong about knowing.
cards.body: In 1963 Edmund Gettier published a short paper that knocked over the three-legged stool from Level 21. His most famous case involves a job, a company president and ten coins.

cards.headline: Smith’s careful reasoning
cards.body: Smith and Jones have both applied for a job. The company president has told Smith that Jones will get it. Smith has also counted the coins in Jones’s pocket: ten. So Smith concludes, carefully and sensibly, that the person who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. No guessing here. Good evidence, good inference.

cards.headline: The twist
cards.body: Then Smith gets the job himself. And, unknown to him, he has ten coins in his own pocket too. So his belief is true, he believes it, and he’s justified. All three legs stand. Yet almost everyone agrees Smith didn’t know it. What made his belief true was luck: facts he had no idea about.

cards.headline: A stool that fell over
cards.body: Gettier’s article had a dramatic impact. Almost all epistemologists agreed that he had refuted the traditional definition of knowledge. Cases like his became known as Gettier cases, and the hunt was on for a fourth condition, JTB plus something, that would finally keep luck out.

cards.headline: Patching the leak
cards.body: One natural patch: a known belief can’t rest on anything false. Smith leaned on a false belief, that Jones would get the job. But this patch isn’t widely accepted, because Gettier cases don’t need false evidence. Luck finds other ways in. In Roderick Chisholm’s sheep in the field, you see what looks exactly like a sheep and believe a sheep is in the field. You’re right: one is hidden behind a hill. What you saw was a dog in disguise.

title: The Ancient Skeptics
objective: After this level you can explain how Pyrrho and Sextus Empiricus balanced opposing arguments and suspended judgment in search of peace of mind.
summary: Pyrrhonian skeptics, recorded by Sextus Empiricus, set equal arguments against each other, suspended judgment and found tranquillity; critics said they could not act.

cards.headline: What if giving up on the answer brought you peace?
cards.body: Most philosophers chase answers. One school of Greek skeptics tried something stranger: weigh every argument against its opposite, stop judging, and see what happens to your worries.

cards.headline: Pyrrho, who wrote nothing
cards.body: The school is named after Pyrrho of Elis, who lived from about 365 to about 275 BCE. He wrote nothing, so we piece him together from other people’s reports. The fullest account comes centuries later, from Sextus Empiricus, probably of the second or third century CE, in his Outlines of Pyrrhonism.

cards.headline: The balancing skill
cards.body: Sextus describes the skeptic’s key ability: for every argument, find an equal and opposing argument. When the two weigh the same, like pans on a level scale, you suspend judgment (in Greek, epoche). Skeptics had phrases for it: “No more this than that” and “I determine nothing”. And then comes the payoff: tranquillity.

cards.headline: The painter’s sponge
cards.body: Sextus explains the payoff with a story. The painter Apelles was trying to paint the foam on a horse’s mouth and kept failing. In frustration he flung his paint-wiping sponge at the picture, and it left a perfect image of the foam. Skeptics set out to find answers, gave up, and found that calm followed anyway.

cards.headline: But how do you get out of bed?
cards.body: Critics pressed the most famous objection, the apraxia charge: without beliefs, you cannot act. Sextus replied that skeptics live by appearances. They are guided by nature, which lets them perceive and think; by feelings, as hunger leads them to food; by the customs and laws they grew up with; and by the skills they were taught.

title: Brain in a Vat
objective: After this level you can explain the brain-in-a-vat puzzle and how Hilary Putnam argued that you cannot coherently think you are one.
summary: The skeptic says you can’t know you’re not a brain in a vat; Putnam argued that, since words refer only through causal links, saying you are one refutes itself.

cards.headline: Can you prove you’re not a brain in a jar?
cards.body: Imagine your brain in a vat, wired to a computer that perfectly simulates the outside world. Everything would feel exactly as it does now. So how could you ever tell?

cards.headline: The skeptic’s argument
cards.body: That’s the brain-in-a-vat puzzle, usually read as a modern version of Descartes’s evil demon who deceives us. The skeptic argues like this. If you know that snow is white, you know you’re not a brain in a vat. But you can’t know you’re not one. So you don’t know that snow is white, or anything else about the outside world.

cards.headline: The ant that drew Churchill
cards.body: In Reason, Truth and History (1981), Hilary Putnam starts with an ant. Crawling on sand, it traces by pure chance a line that looks like a caricature of Winston Churchill. Has it drawn Churchill? Most people say no: the ant has never seen him. For Putnam, words work the same way. A word refers to something only through the right causal connection to it.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: Putnam grants the vat world is physically possible. His claim is that you can’t truly say or think you live in one.

cards.headline: The sentence that undoes itself
cards.body: Now Putnam’s version: suppose every thinking being is a brain in a vat, run by a computer with no programmer. Their word “vat” was never caused by real vats, so it doesn’t refer to them. So if they say “We are brains in a vat”, it comes out false. The sentence refutes itself, Putnam argued, like “All general statements are false”.

cards.headline: The loophole
cards.body: Critics doubt this defeats the skeptic. Crispin Wright argued in 1994 that Putnam’s argument leaves some nightmares untouched, such as your brain being taken out of your skull last night and hooked up to a computer. The old worry survives in a new form.

title: Knowing Without Looking
objective: After this level you can tell a priori knowledge, known by reason alone, from a posteriori knowledge, known through experience.
summary: A priori knowledge is known by reason alone, independently of experience; a posteriori knowledge rests on experience. Mill argued even arithmetic is learned from experience.

cards.headline: You know no bachelor is married. Have you checked?
cards.body: Nobody has surveyed every bachelor on Earth, yet you’re sure none of them is married. Knowing it’s raining outside works quite differently: someone has to look. Two routes to knowing.

cards.headline: Two routes
cards.body: Philosophers call the first route a priori: knowable independently of experience, apart from the experience of learning the words. The second is a posteriori: known on the basis of experience. “All bachelors are unmarried” is the classic a priori example. “It is raining outside” is a posteriori, since someone has to experience the weather.

points: Water is H2O

cards.headline: How reason does it
cards.body: How can thinking alone justify a belief? Once you understand the terms, you seem able to see the truth just by reflecting on what the claim says. When seven is added to five, the sum must be twelve; no counting apples required. That’s why a priori justification is described as coming from pure thought or reason.

cards.headline: Mill’s challenge
cards.body: Not everyone accepts that arithmetic is known this way. John Stuart Mill held that even the laws of arithmetic and geometry are learned by induction from experience, like other laws of nature. Critics such as A. J. Ayer replied that this would make “2 + 2 = 4” an uncertain, contingent truth, open to revision like any finding about the world.

title: Why Expect the Sun to Rise?
objective: After this level you can explain Hume's problem of induction: why any argument that the future will resemble the past seems to assume what it needs to prove.
summary: Hume argued that no argument can show the future will resemble the past without assuming it; we expect it from custom, and Reichenbach later offered a pragmatic vindication.

cards.headline: The sun has risen every day of your life. So what?
cards.body: You’re sure it will rise tomorrow. David Hume asked an unsettling question: what reasoning actually gets you from all those past mornings to the next one?

cards.headline: Darkness isn’t a contradiction
cards.body: In his Enquiry of 1748, Hume wrote: “That the sun will not rise to-morrow is no less intelligible a proposition, and implies no more contradiction than the affirmation, that it will rise.” His homelier example was bread. The bread he ate before nourished him. Does it follow that other bread must nourish him at another time? “The consequence seems nowise necessary.”

mascot.line: It connects: this is Level 25’s split again. Reason alone can’t prove it, and experience would argue in a circle.

cards.headline: A trap with two doors
cards.body: Hume’s argument is a dilemma. Any argument that the future will resemble the past is either demonstrative, proved by reason alone, or probable, drawn from experience. Not demonstrative: nature changing course implies no contradiction. And a probable argument from experience already assumes the future resembles the past, “taking that for granted, which is the very point in question”.

cards.headline: Custom, the great guide
cards.body: Hume never told anyone to stop expecting sunrises. We do draw these inferences, he said, but custom or habit draws them, not reasoning. See flame and heat together often enough, and the mind is carried by custom to expect heat from the next flame. “Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.”

cards.headline: Reichenbach’s bet
cards.body: Later philosophers kept trying. Hans Reichenbach accepted Hume’s argument but offered a weaker, pragmatic vindication. We can’t show that induction will succeed, but if any method of prediction works, induction does. He compared it to a physician who says: I don’t know whether an operation will save this man, but if any remedy will, the operation will.

title: Nyaya's Sources of Knowledge
objective: After this level you can explain the Nyaya school's four sources of knowledge, including its classic inference from smoke on a hill to fire.
summary: Nyaya’s four means of knowledge are perception, inference, comparison and testimony; its five-step inference from smoke to fire rests on a pervasion the Carvakas doubted.

cards.headline: Where there’s smoke, there’s a theory of knowledge.
cards.body: Level 9 met the Nyaya school and its model inference: smoke on the hill, so fire on the hill. Now look inside the machine. How exactly does Nyaya get from smoke you can see to fire you can’t?

cards.headline: Four ways to know
cards.body: Nyaya counts four pramanas, or means of knowledge: perception, inference, comparison and testimony. Perception is called the “eldest”, because the others all depend on its input. Testimony is the word of a qualified speaker: someone with direct knowledge who is willing to pass it on without distortion.

cards.headline: Comparison, with a buffalo
cards.body: Comparison sounds vague until you meet the stock example. Someone is told that a water buffalo looks something like a cow. Later, in the countryside, he sees an animal like a cow and recognizes it: that’s a water buffalo. Nyaya treats this as its own way of knowing, used mostly for learning what words name.

cards.headline: Five steps to fire
cards.body: When arguing with others, Nyaya lays inference out in five steps. There is fire on the hill. Because there is smoke on the hill. Wherever there is smoke there is fire, like a kitchen hearth and unlike a lake. This hill is likewise smoky. So there is fire on the hill. The third step carries the weight: the pervasion, vyapti, the rule that smoke never comes without fire.

mascot.line: It connects: the Carvakas pressed their own version of the puzzle about generalizing that Level 26 met in Hume.

cards.headline: The Carvakas push back
cards.body: The Carvaka materialists attacked that third step. Inference, they argued, depends on generalizations that outrun anything perceived: nobody can know that every case of smoke comes with fire. The standard reply was practical. We couldn’t act as we do without inference, and the skeptic relies on generalizations the moment he speaks, using words with repeatable meanings.

title: What Makes a Belief True?
objective: After this level you can compare the correspondence theory of truth, matching the world, with the coherence theory, fitting with other beliefs.
summary: The correspondence theory says a belief is true when it matches the world; the coherence theory says it is true when it fits with other beliefs. Each faces a classic objection.

cards.headline: Pink elephants on the highway. True or false?
cards.body: A drunk driver swears pink elephants are dancing on the road ahead. You’re sure he’s wrong. But what exactly makes his claim false? Two classic theories of truth give different answers.

cards.headline: Truth as matching
cards.body: The correspondence theory says a belief is true when it corresponds to a fact, to the way the world is. It is often traced to Aristotle’s Metaphysics: “To say of what is that it is not, or of what is not that it is, is false, while to say of what is that it is, and of what is not that it is not, is true.” Truth is a match between belief and world.

cards.headline: Truth as fitting
cards.body: The coherence theory says a belief is true when it coheres, or fits, with a specified set of other beliefs. Watch how you judge the driver. Elephants are gray. There’s no zoo or circus nearby. Nobody else sees them. His claim fails to fit with all that, so you reject it as false, and take away the car keys.

cards.headline: Can you step outside your head?
cards.body: A popular objection to correspondence: we can’t step outside our own minds to compare our thoughts with reality itself. If truth were matching, we could never check the match, and knowledge would be impossible. British idealists around 1900, such as F. H. Bradley, adopted a coherence theory instead.

cards.headline: A good story fits too
cards.body: Bertrand Russell objected to coherence in 1907. “Jane Austen was hanged for murder” coheres with some set of propositions, just as “Jane Austen died in her bed” coheres with another. Fitting alone can’t pick the true one. Coherence theorists reply that truth is coherence with the beliefs we actually hold, not with any set you can invent.

title: Truth That Works
objective: After this level you can explain how the American pragmatists Peirce, James and Dewey tied truth and meaning to practical consequences.
summary: The American pragmatists tied meaning and truth to practical consequences: Peirce’s maxim and truth as the end of inquiry, James’s expedient belief, Dewey’s inquiry as problem solving.

cards.headline: What difference would it make if it were true?
cards.body: A group of American philosophers asked that about every idea. Their movement, pragmatism, began in the United States around 1870, and tied meaning and truth to practical consequences.

cards.headline: Peirce’s test for meaning
cards.body: Charles Sanders Peirce stated pragmatism’s maxim in 1878. To get clear about an idea, consider the practical effects you conceive its object to have; your idea of those effects is your whole idea of it. His first example: calling something hard means that many other substances won’t scratch it. No effects, no meaning.

cards.headline: Truth at the end of inquiry
cards.body: Peirce applied the test to truth itself. The truth, he wrote, is “the opinion which is fated to be ultimately agreed to by all who investigate”. So truth is the goal of inquiry: what careful investigation would settle on in the long run.

cards.headline: James: truth that pays its way
cards.body: William James, Peirce’s friend, turned pragmatism into a theory of truth in Pragmatism (1907). “The true”, he wrote, “is only the expedient in the way of our thinking”, expedient in the long run and on the whole. Ideas become true as they help us get into satisfactory relation with the rest of our experience.

cards.headline: Dewey’s toolbox
cards.body: John Dewey, leader of the next generation, saw inquiry as beginning with a problem and aiming to resolve it. The logical forms we use along the way are instruments: tools for solving the problem.

cards.headline: The Santa Claus objection
cards.body: Bertrand Russell objected that James was committed to the truth of “Santa Claus exists”, since believing it can make people happy. Defenders call that unfair: on James’s view, a comforting belief is only wholly true if it doesn’t clash with other vital benefits.

In 1868 Peirce wrote: “Let us not pretend to doubt in philosophy what we do not doubt in our hearts.” Real doubt needs a positive reason. Yet he was a fallibilist: at any point inquiry is provisional, and we can’t tell how far we are from the truth.

cards.headline: Still no agreed definition
cards.body: And knowledge itself? After Gettier, epistemologists poured effort into repairing the three-part definition, especially in the late 20th century, but no analysis has been widely accepted. Some now doubt knowledge can be broken into parts at all. The question Socrates pressed in Plato’s Theaetetus is still open.

title: The Mind-Body Problem
objective: After this level you can explain the mind-body problem: how thoughts and feelings relate to the physical brain and body.
summary: The mind-body problem asks how thoughts and feelings relate to a physical body, both what minds are and how the two affect each other; dualism, materialism and idealism are the classic answers.

cards.headline: A decision weighs nothing. So how does it lift your arm?
cards.body: You decide to ask a question, and up goes your hand. The decision has no size or weight, yet a very physical arm obeys it. Philosophers call the puzzle behind that everyday moment the mind-body problem.

cards.headline: Two very different lists
cards.body: Make two lists about yourself. On the first go your size, weight, shape and motion: physical properties, the kind physics measures. On the second go what you perceive, what you feel, what you believe and what you want: mental properties, which nobody thinks a rock has. The mind-body problem asks how one being can carry both lists, when the two seem so closely linked.

cards.headline: Two questions in one
cards.body: The problem splits in two. First, what are minds and bodies? Is the mind nothing over and above the body, or something else entirely? Second, how do they affect each other? Your decision seems to move your arm. Your sense organs, which are physical, give you sensations, which are mental. Explaining that traffic in both directions is where the trouble starts.

cards.headline: Three classic answers
cards.body: Philosophers have three classic answers. Dualists say mind and body are both real and fundamentally different kinds of thing. Materialists, also called physicalists, say the mind is fundamentally physical. Idealists flip that around: matter is fundamentally mental. The next few levels put dualism and physicalism on trial, one objection at a time.

title: The Ghost in the Machine
objective: After this level you can explain Descartes's dualism of mind and matter, Princess Elisabeth's question about how they interact, and Ryle's nickname for it.
summary: Descartes held the mind is a thinking, unextended thing distinct from the body; Elisabeth asked how such a mind could move a body, and Ryle mocked the view as the ghost in the machine.

cards.headline: Is there a ghost steering your body?
cards.body: Descartes said your mind and your body are two different things. A princess asked him how they could ever touch. Three centuries later, a philosopher gave his view a mocking nickname.

cards.headline: Two kinds of thing
cards.body: René Descartes argued that the mind is a thinking thing with no extension: it takes up no space. The body is the reverse, an extended thing that doesn’t think. Since their natures are so different, he concluded they are really distinct, and one could exist without the other. He added that a body can always be divided into parts, while he could find no parts in himself as a thinking thing. This is mind-body dualism.

cards.headline: A princess asks the obvious question
cards.body: In 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia began writing to Descartes with a sharp question: how can a soul that is only a thinking thing move a body? Her worry went like this. To set something moving, a thing has to come into contact with it, like one pool ball striking another. Contact needs a surface, and a mind with no extension has none. How does a ghost push a button?

cards.headline: Ryle names the ghost
cards.body: In The Concept of Mind (1949), Gilbert Ryle called the Cartesian picture, “with deliberate abusiveness”, “the dogma of the Ghost in the Machine”. His diagnosis was a category mistake: the dogma treats the facts of mental life as if they belonged to one logical category, when they belong to another. On Ryle’s diagnosis, Descartes filed the mind on the wrong shelf.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: Ryle never said people don’t think. He said the mind isn’t an extra thing hiding inside the body.

cards.headline: “But where is the University?”
cards.body: Ryle’s example: a visitor to Oxford or Cambridge is shown the colleges, libraries and offices, then asks, “But where is the University?” The University isn’t one more building. It’s the way all of them are organized. Ryle wasn’t denying that people think: doing long division is a mental process, he said, and so is making a joke. What he denied was a hidden extra thing doing it.

title: The Mind Is the Brain
objective: After this level you can explain the identity theory, the physicalist view that each mental state simply is a brain state.
summary: The identity theory holds that each mental state simply is a brain state, as lightning is an electrical discharge; Putnam objected that octopuses feel pain with very different brains.

cards.headline: What if your pain is a brain event, and nothing more?
cards.body: Not caused by the brain. Not linked to it. The very same thing. In the 1950s a few philosophers made that bold claim, and they defended it with lightning.

cards.headline: The mind is the brain
cards.body: The identity theory took shape in U.T. Place’s 1956 paper “Is Consciousness a Brain Process?”, and in work by Herbert Feigl and J.J.C. Smart. Its claim: an experience of pain, or of seeing something, just is a process in the brain. Not merely correlated with one, but identical to it. That makes it a form of physicalism.

cards.headline: Lightning, twice named
cards.body: Critics objected that “sensation” doesn’t mean “brain process”. Place agreed, and pointed to lightning. “Lightning” doesn’t mean “a motion of electric charges” either. You find out that something is lightning by looking, and that it’s an electrical discharge by theory and experiment. Two words, two routes, one thing. Sensations and brain processes, he argued, could be the same way.

cards.headline: Found out, not defined
cards.body: So the identity is a discovery, not a definition. Nobody could work it out from the meaning of the words; science had to find it. So it’s no embarrassment that earlier thinkers missed it. Aristotle, after all, thought the brain was for cooling the blood.

cards.headline: The octopus objection
cards.body: In 1967 Hilary Putnam objected. Mammals, birds, reptiles and even mollusks such as octopuses all seem able to feel pain, yet their brains differ enormously. If pain just is one kind of brain state, they would all need that same state. David Lewis replied that identities can be local: pain may be one brain state in human nervous systems and another in mollusk ones.

title: Minds as Software
objective: After this level you can explain functionalism, which defines mental states by what they do, and why it allows minds made of something other than neurons.
summary: Functionalism defines a mental state by its role between inputs, other states and behavior, not by what it is made of, so minds could run on silicon; Ned Block’s Chinese nation challenges it.

cards.headline: What makes a key a key?
cards.body: Not the metal. A wooden key or a plastic one does the job just as well, as long as it opens the lock. Some philosophers think minds work the same way.

cards.headline: Defined by the job
cards.body: Functionalism says a mental state is defined by what it does, not what it’s made of. A key is anything that can open the lock. Likewise, a thought, a desire or a pain is whatever plays the right role: the right links to what comes in through the senses, to other mental states, and to what the body does next.

mascot.line: It connects: Level 33 asked what pain is made of. Functionalism asks what pain does. That switch is the whole theory.

cards.headline: Pain’s job description
cards.body: A simple functionalist theory describes pain this way: the state caused by bodily injury that produces the belief that something is wrong, the desire to be out of that state, anxiety, and wincing or moaning. In humans, some neural activity, perhaps C-fiber stimulation, plays that role. In a hypothetical Martian or android, a silicon-based state could play it instead. Both would count as pain.

cards.headline: The software picture
cards.body: Where did the idea come from? Hilary Putnam modeled mental states on computing machines, where a program fixes how inputs and internal states lead to outputs, and he defended functionalism as a full theory in 1967. Hence the popular picture of the mind as software running on the brain’s hardware, though it’s only an analogy. The same program can run on very different machines.

cards.headline: A nation-sized brain
cards.body: Ned Block pushed back with a vast thought experiment. Imagine the whole population of China organized to copy a brain’s functional organization, each person acting like a neuron. By functionalism’s lights, that system would have a mind. Block argues it would have no experiences at all. Daniel Dennett replied that such cases only trouble crude functional theories.

title: Can Machines Think?
objective: After this level you can explain Alan Turing's 1950 imitation game and what passing it would and would not show.
summary: Turing’s 1950 imitation game asks whether a machine’s typed answers can fool an interrogator; the argument from consciousness and Block’s Blockhead ask what passing would show.

cards.headline: Can machines think? Turing thought that was the wrong question.
cards.body: In 1950 he swapped it for a game you could actually play.

cards.headline: The imitation game
cards.body: Picture three players. An interrogator sits in a separate room and puts questions to two hidden players, who answer in typed text, so tone of voice can’t help. In Turing’s first version, the task is to tell which player is the man and which is the woman. Then comes the twist: a machine takes one of the seats. Can the interrogator still tell?

cards.headline: Turing’s bet
cards.body: In “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, Turing called “Can machines think?” too meaningless to deserve discussion. His game offered a sharper target. He predicted that in about 50 years, computers would play so well that an average interrogator would have no more than a 70 percent chance of picking correctly after five minutes of questions.

cards.headline: But does it feel anything?
cards.body: Turing tackled objections himself. Professor Jefferson had argued in 1949 that a machine must feel its thoughts, not merely produce symbols. Turing replied that, strictly, you can’t be sure anyone but you thinks either. You judge others by how they respond, and keep what he called “the polite convention that everyone thinks”. Why not extend it to machines?

cards.headline: The giant look-up table
cards.body: So what would passing show? Ned Block imagined “Blockhead”, run by a vast look-up tree with a programmed reply stored for every possible input. It could answer every question just as you would, while only looking things up. Critics take Blockhead to show that passing the test isn’t enough for intelligence: it gives the right answers without thinking them through.

title: The Chinese Room
objective: After this level you can explain John Searle's Chinese room and his argument that following rules for symbols is not the same as understanding.
summary: Searle’s 1980 Chinese room argues that following rules for symbols is not understanding them, so a program alone can’t produce understanding; the systems reply says the whole room understands.

cards.headline: Can you answer in Chinese without knowing a word of it?
cards.body: In 1980 John Searle built an imaginary room to test whether running a program is the same as understanding.

cards.headline: The room
cards.body: Searle imagines himself alone in a room. Chinese characters are slipped under the door. He understands no Chinese, but he has a program, written in English, telling him which characters to send back out. He follows it perfectly. Outside, people read his replies and conclude there’s a Chinese speaker inside. There isn’t. There’s a man following rules.

cards.headline: Symbols without meaning
cards.body: That, Searle says, is all a computer does: it manipulates symbols by their syntax, their shapes and rules, without grasping their meaning, their semantics. If the man can run the program without understanding Chinese, then running a program can’t by itself produce understanding. And fooling the people outside, as in Turing’s test, isn’t enough to show understanding.

cards.headline: Not an anti-machine argument
cards.body: Searle’s target was what he called Strong AI: the claim that a suitably programmed computer really understands. He wasn’t saying no machine can think. Brains are machines, he said, and brains think. His point was narrower: the right program, on its own, isn’t what makes a mind.

cards.headline: The systems reply
cards.body: The reply Searle called perhaps the most common: fine, the man doesn’t understand Chinese, but he’s only one part. The whole system, man plus rulebook plus scraps of paper, understands. Searle’s answer: let the man memorize the rules and do everything in his head. Now he is the whole system, and he still doesn’t know what a single character means.

title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
objective: After this level you can explain Thomas Nagel's argument that science's outside view may leave out what an experience is like from the inside.
summary: Nagel argued in 1974 that a creature is conscious if there is something it is like to be it, and that an objective view may leave out that inner viewpoint; Akins replied from bat neuroscience.

cards.headline: Learn every fact about a bat’s brain. Would you know what being one is like?
cards.body: In 1974 Thomas Nagel picked the bat on purpose: its world arrives by echo.

cards.headline: Something it is like
cards.body: Nagel’s test for consciousness is short. An organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism, for the organism itself. He called this the subjective character of experience. It’s the inside view: not what your brain is doing, but how things are for you.

cards.headline: Try being a bat
cards.body: Most bats find their way by sonar, reading the echoes of their own high-pitched shrieks, a sense unlike any of ours. So try to imagine it. Webbed arms, poor eyesight, a day spent hanging upside down in an attic. Nagel’s verdict: that only tells you what it would be like for you to behave like a bat. It doesn’t tell you what it is like for a bat to be a bat.

cards.headline: The view from outside
cards.body: Here’s the problem for physicalism. Every subjective experience, Nagel argued, is tied to a single point of view. An objective, physical theory describes things in a way that doesn’t depend on any one point of view, so it seems bound to leave out exactly what makes an experience an experience. Yet Nagel said it would be a mistake to conclude that physicalism is false. We just have no idea yet how it could be true.

cards.headline: Study the bat
cards.body: Critics pushed back with science. Kathleen Akins dug into bat physiology and argued that many questions about a bat’s experience that seem hopelessly open actually turn on details of the bat’s brain that neuroscientists haven’t worked out yet.

title: Mary's Room
objective: After this level you can explain Frank Jackson's Mary, who knows every physical fact about color, and the debate over whether she learns something new on seeing red.
summary: Jackson’s Mary knows every physical fact about color but has never seen it; if seeing red teaches her something, not all information is physical, but the ability reply says she gains know-how.

cards.headline: She knows everything about red. She has never seen it.
cards.body: Frank Jackson’s 1982 thought experiment locks a scientist in a black and white room, then opens the door.

cards.headline: The black and white room
cards.body: Mary is a brilliant scientist who investigates the world from a black and white room, through a black and white television. Her specialty is the science of vision. She learns all the physical information there is about what happens when we see ripe tomatoes or the sky: which wavelengths stimulate the retina, and exactly how that leads someone to say “The sky is blue”. She has simply never seen color herself.

cards.headline: What happens at the door?
cards.body: Then Mary is released, or given a color screen. Does she learn anything? Jackson said it seems obvious she does: she learns what seeing red is like. But then her physical knowledge was incomplete, even though she had all of it. So, he concluded, not all information is physical information, and physicalism is false.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: this reply doesn’t deny that Mary gains something. It says what she gains is know-how, not a new fact.

cards.headline: A skill, not a fact
cards.body: The best-known reply is the ability hypothesis, defended by David Lewis and Laurence Nemirow. Mary does gain something, they say, but it isn’t a new fact. It’s a bundle of abilities: to imagine red, to remember it, to recognize it when she sees it again. Knowing what red is like is know-how, like riding a bike, not one more item for her notebook.

cards.headline: The author changes sides
cards.body: Here’s a twist. Jackson himself later changed his mind. He came to argue that something must be wrong with his own knowledge argument, and he now defends physicalism. Others still defend Mary’s room, so the argument lives on without its author.
