title: When Words Make Puzzles
objective: After this level you can explain the later Wittgenstein's idea that meaning is use and why he thought some philosophical puzzles come from language misfiring.
summary: The later Wittgenstein held that meaning is often use, that ’game’ is joined by family resemblance, and that some puzzles come from language misleading us; Russell was unimpressed.

cards.headline: Try defining “game.” Every definition breaks.
cards.body: Chess, tag, solitaire, catch. Ludwig Wittgenstein thought that your trouble finding the one thing they all share tells you something about meaning, and about philosophy.

cards.headline: Meaning is use
cards.body: Wittgenstein’s Philosophical Investigations was published in 1953, after his death. For a large class of cases, it says, “the meaning of a word is its use in the language.” So don’t hunt for an object the word names, or a feeling in the speaker’s head. Look at what people do with the word.

cards.headline: A toolbox of words
cards.body: “Think of the tools in a tool-box,” he writes: a hammer, pliers, a saw, a screwdriver, a glue-pot. The functions of words are just as varied. And games? Look closely and you find no single feature common to them all, only “a complicated network of similarities overlapping and criss-crossing.” He called these family resemblances.

cards.headline: When language misfires
cards.body: Wittgenstein thought many philosophical puzzles come from being misled by the surface of words. “I’ll keep it in mind” sounds like “I’ll keep it in this box,” and suddenly the mind looks like a mysterious box with contents. The cure is to recall how we actually use words like mind and memory. Philosophy’s aim, he wrote, is “to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle.”

cards.headline: Not everyone was won over
cards.body: His former teacher Bertrand Russell was blunt. In 1959 he wrote that he had not found in the Investigations “anything that seemed to me interesting,” and couldn’t see why a whole school found important wisdom in its pages. Others disagree strongly: Wittgenstein is counted among the most influential philosophers of the twentieth century, by some the most important since Kant.

title: The Trolley Problem
objective: After this level you can explain Philippa Foot’s trolley problem and use it to test whether saving five by diverting harm to one is allowed.
summary: Foot’s runaway tram and her judge case trade one for five yet get different verdicts; her doing/allowing explanation was tested by Thomson’s bystander, and Thomson later changed her mind.

cards.headline: Five on one track, one on the other. You’re steering.
cards.body: In 1967 Philippa Foot built a small case to test a big question: may you divert harm onto one person to save five?

cards.headline: Foot’s runaway tram
cards.body: Philippa Foot imagined the driver of a runaway tram. He can’t stop it; he can only steer from one track to another. Five people are on one track, one person on the other. Foot held that the driver may steer toward the one. It sounds like simple arithmetic: five is more than one. Her next case shows why it isn’t.

cards.headline: The judge next door
cards.body: Foot set the tram beside a darker case. Rioters will kill five people unless a culprit is found, and a judge could stop them only by framing one innocent man. The trade is again one for five. Yet Foot held that the judge must not do it, while the driver may steer. Same numbers, opposite verdicts. Whatever decides these cases, it isn’t only counting.

mascot.line: People mix these up: the tram driver is Foot’s case. The bystander at the switch is Thomson’s twist on it.

cards.headline: Doing versus allowing
cards.body: Foot’s explanation: the judge chooses between killing one and allowing five to die, and not harming weighs more than helping. The driver chooses between killing one and killing five, so fewer deaths wins. Then Judith Jarvis Thomson swapped the driver for a bystander at a switch. The bystander would kill one rather than let five die, yet turning still seemed permissible to many. Foot’s explanation wobbled.

cards.headline: Thomson changes her mind
cards.body: Thomson later argued against the consensus that the bystander may turn. In 2008 she asked: would you turn the trolley onto yourself? Few would. Then, she argued, you may not turn it onto a stranger either, just as you may not steal someone’s wallet to give to charity. Her critics hold to the older consensus. The lever is still argued over.

title: The Footbridge
objective: After this level you can explain why many people who would pull the switch refuse to push a man off a footbridge, and how the doctrine of double effect tries to explain the difference.
summary: Thomson’s footbridge keeps five for one, yet many who would switch refuse to push; double effect explains it by intended means versus foreseen side effect, and critics raise the problem of closeness.

cards.headline: Same five, same one. Why does pushing feel so different from pulling?
cards.body: Many people who would pull a lever to save five refuse to push one person to do it. The count hasn’t changed. Something else has.

cards.headline: Thomson’s footbridge
cards.body: Judith Jarvis Thomson set out the case in 1985, building on Foot’s examples from 1967. A trolley is heading for five people who can’t escape. You’re on a footbridge above the track, next to a heavy stranger. The only way to stop the trolley is to push him off, onto the track. The trade is exactly the switch case’s: one for five.

cards.headline: Many say no
cards.body: Many people believe pushing him would be wrong, yet switching the trolley onto a track with one person would be permissible. If only the number of lives mattered, the two cases would get the same answer. So philosophers set out to name the difference that seems to be doing the work.

cards.headline: Means or side effect?
cards.body: One answer is the doctrine of double effect, credited to Thomas Aquinas. It separates harm you cause as a means to a good end from harm you cause only as a foreseen side effect. At the switch, the one person’s death is a foreseen side effect of diverting the trolley. On the bridge, his body stopping the trolley is the plan itself. On this view, that makes pushing wrong.

cards.headline: Critics push back
cards.body: Critics raise the problem of closeness. Some harms sit so close to the means that it’s hard to call them merely foreseen, and no clear way of drawing that line has emerged. Others split differently: some take the switch and push intuitions as proof of double effect, Thomson in 2008 denied that switching is allowed at all, and McIntyre denied that double effect explains the switch case.

title: The Drowning Child
objective: After this level you can apply Peter Singer’s drowning child argument to the question of how much we owe distant strangers, and weigh the main replies.
summary: Singer’s 1972 shallow pond supports a rescue principle he applies to distant suffering; critics press the demandingness objection.

cards.headline: You’d ruin your clothes to save a drowning child. Peter Singer has a follow-up.
cards.body: Almost everyone answers the first question the same way. Singer’s 1972 essay asks what that answer commits you to.

cards.headline: The shallow pond
cards.body: In “Famine, Affluence, and Morality” (1972), Peter Singer pictures walking past a shallow pond and seeing a child drowning. You ought to wade in, he says, even though your clothes get muddy. The mud is insignificant; the child’s death would be very bad. Walking past strikes most people as monstrous. So far, nobody argues.

cards.headline: From pond to principle
cards.body: Singer’s argument runs on premises. If it is in our power to prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything morally significant, we ought to do it. Suffering and death from lack of food, shelter or medical care are very bad. We can prevent some of it by giving. So, he concludes, we are all like the person passing the pond: the cost of a new shirt or a night out can mean the difference between life and death for someone elsewhere.

cards.headline: Far away still counts
cards.body: Singer argued that distance makes no moral difference. A person in need far away counts as much as the child in front of you, because what matters is your ability to help at little cost to yourself. The pond is just the case where you can’t miss it.

cards.headline: Too much to ask?
cards.body: A common criticism is the demandingness objection. Commonsense morality treats charity as good but optional, critics say, and the world’s needs never stop: a pond you pass once is not a world of endless ponds, and helping every time would take over your life. Singer’s defenders reply that his moderate principle asks you to give up only what isn’t morally significant, which leaves room for the projects that matter most to you.

title: Can They Suffer?
objective: After this level you can weigh the arguments of Bentham, Singer and their critics about whether animals’ suffering counts morally as much as ours.
summary: Bentham made suffering the test and Singer asked for equal consideration of like interests; Aristotle and Kant ranked animals lower, and critics reply.

cards.headline: Can it reason? Can it talk? Bentham thought those were the wrong questions.
cards.body: Where does the moral circle end? In 1789 Jeremy Bentham proposed a test that still divides philosophers.

cards.headline: Bentham’s question
cards.body: Jeremy Bentham asked what should mark the line between beings whose interests count and mere things. Not the faculty of reason, not the faculty of speech. “The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?” If a being can suffer, its suffering is something morality has to weigh.

cards.headline: Equal weight for like interests
cards.body: Peter Singer built on Bentham. His principle of equal consideration of interests gives equal weight to the like interests of all those affected by our actions, whatever their species. Favoring your own species just because it is yours has a name: speciesism, coined by Richard Ryder in the 1970s as a prejudice he compared to racism, and popularized by Singer.

cards.headline: The other side
cards.body: Aristotle ranked living beings by their abilities. Humans can use reason to guide conduct; animals rely on instinct, so, he held, the function of animals is to serve the needs of human beings. Kant denied that we have direct duties to animals. Yet he condemned cruelty, because “he who is cruel to animals becomes hard also in his dealings with men.” Our duties regarding animals, for Kant, are owed to humanity.

cards.headline: Whose wrong is it?
cards.body: Critics find the indirect view unsatisfying. It makes cruelty to an animal wrong because of what it does to the person, and so, they argue, it fails to capture the wrong done to the animal itself. Indirect theorists reply that even without direct moral status for animals, we can still have demanding duties regarding how we treat them, starting with a duty not to be cruel.

title: The Murderer at the Door
objective: After this level you can weigh Kant’s claim that you may not lie even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding against a consequentialist reply.
summary: Constant held truth is owed only to those with a right to it; Kant replied in 1797 that truthfulness is unconditional; consequentialists allow a protective lie.

cards.headline: A murderer knocks and asks if your friend is hiding inside. May you lie?
cards.body: In 1797 two thinkers argued over exactly this doorstep. One of them said no.

cards.headline: Constant’s challenge
cards.body: In 1797 Benjamin Constant attacked a German philosopher who held that lying to a murderer, asking whether your friend had taken refuge in your house, would be a crime. A duty to tell the truth, taken unconditionally, would make society impossible, Constant wrote. Truth is owed only to someone with a right to it, and no one has a right to a truth that injures others.

cards.headline: Kant answers
cards.body: Kant replied in an essay the same year. Truthfulness in statements you can’t avoid is a duty to everyone, however great the disadvantage to you or anyone else. A lie always injures someone: if not a particular person, then humanity, because it makes declarations in general less trustworthy. To be truthful, he wrote, is “a sacred unconditional command of reason”.

cards.headline: Kant turns the tables
cards.body: Kant even used consequences against the liar. Suppose you say your friend isn’t home, but he has slipped out unseen and meets the murderer on his way. Then, Kant argued, you could justly be accused as the cause. Whoever lies must answer for what follows. Tell the truth, and the outcome isn’t charged to you.

cards.headline: The consequentialist reply
cards.body: Consequentialists hold that whether an act is right depends only on its consequences. From Constant to Mill and Sidgwick, many philosophers have held that lying to a would-be murderer is permitted: on this view, a lie that protects a life is the better act. Kant’s answer is that even one exception undermines the trust on which every right founded on contract depends.

title: Moral Luck
objective: After this level you can explain Bernard Williams’s and Thomas Nagel’s puzzle of moral luck, using two equally careless drivers with different outcomes.
summary: Williams and Nagel showed that our blame depends on luck, clashing with the Control Principle; some deny moral luck by locating blame in intentions, and Nagel replied that luck reaches intentions too.

cards.headline: Two drivers make the same mistake. Only one of them is unlucky.
cards.body: Should we blame them differently? Most of us do. Two philosophers asked whether we should.

cards.headline: A phrase that shouldn’t work
cards.body: In 1976 Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel published a now classic pair of papers, both called “Moral Luck”. Williams expected the phrase to sound like an oxymoron. Morality is supposed to be the part of life luck can’t reach. Kant wrote that a good will, even if it achieved nothing, would still shine like a jewel by itself.

cards.headline: The Control Principle
cards.body: Here’s a principle most people find compelling: you are morally assessable only for what depends on factors under your control. If someone steps on your toes because she was pushed, the urge to blame her evaporates. It follows that two people who differ only in factors beyond their control shouldn’t be judged differently.

mascot.line: Keep this: same carelessness, different outcome. The whole puzzle lives in that gap.

cards.headline: Two careless drivers
cards.body: Now take two otherwise careful drivers who both forgot to have their brakes checked. Both brakes fail. Only one finds a child in the path of the car. Their carelessness was identical; only the outcome differed. Judge them differently and you clash with the Control Principle. Nagel identified four kinds of moral luck, and this one is now called resultant luck: luck in how things turn out.

cards.headline: Deny it, or accept it?
cards.body: Some deny that luck changes what anyone deserves. Adam Smith held that all praise and blame ultimately belong to the intention of the heart, and many philosophers say luck changes only how clearly we can see someone’s fault. Nagel replied that luck shapes our intentions too, through circumstances and character, so retreating inward doesn’t escape it.

title: Family First or Everyone Equal?
objective: After this level you can weigh Mozi’s impartial care for all against the Confucian view that love rightly starts with your own family.
summary: The Mohists argued for inclusive care (jian ai) from its consequences and a journey test; Mencius defended care with distinctions that grows outward from the family.

cards.headline: Your nephew or a neighbor’s baby: should you care about them equally?
cards.body: Remember the Mohists from Level 6, who attacked lavish funerals? Their deepest quarrel with the Confucians was about whom to care for.

cards.headline: Inclusive care
cards.body: The Mohists’ best-known teaching is jian ai, usually rendered “inclusive care” or “impartial concern”: care for others without distinguishing self and others, associates and strangers. Their argument ran on consequences. Crime, strife and war come from caring for your own family, city or state and not for others’. If people were for others’ states as for their own, they asked, who would attack another state?

cards.headline: The long journey test
cards.body: The Mohists added a thought experiment. You are leaving on a long journey and must entrust your family to someone. Will you choose a person who cares for everyone impartially, or one who favors their own? Even partial people, the Mohists claimed, would pick the impartial carer.

cards.headline: Love starts at home
cards.body: Confucians held a doctrine of care with distinctions. The Analects calls filial piety the root of goodness, and Mencius taught that benevolence grows by extending the love first shown in the family. He asked the Mohist Yi Zhi whether he truly held that affection for his own nephew is like affection for a neighbor’s baby. Humans naturally care more for relatives, Mencius argued, so a doctrine demanding impartiality is impractical.

cards.headline: Barbs and replies
cards.body: Mencius went further, equating inclusive care with renouncing one’s father and dismissing Mozi as a “beast”. The Mohists replied that impartial concern is no harder than things rulers had already demanded and got from their subjects. Chad Hansen and Bryan Van Norden point to a gap in the journey test: it shows partial people want others to be impartial, not that they should be impartial themselves.

title: Do We Owe Future People?
objective: After this level you can explain why duties to people not yet born are puzzling, including Parfit’s non-identity problem, and apply it to a long-term choice.
summary: A different choice brings different people into existence, so Parfit’s depletion case seems to harm no one yet seems wrong; replies disagree.

cards.headline: Can you harm someone whose very existence depends on your choice?
cards.body: It sounds like a riddle. Derek Parfit showed it is a real problem for any choice that reaches far into the future.

cards.headline: You almost weren’t
cards.body: Had your parents delayed having a child by a few months, the odds are that a different person would exist instead of you. Gregory Kavka called this the precariousness of existence. Derek Parfit, in his 1984 book Reasons and Persons, saw that it turns long-term choices into a puzzle.

cards.headline: Depletion
cards.body: Parfit’s case: a community chooses to deplete a resource rather than conserve it. For two centuries life is slightly better; after that, much lower. But the choice also changes who gets conceived, so the later people would never have existed under conservation. If their lives are still worth living, depletion seems to make none of them worse off.

mascot.line: Don’t memorize the dates. Remember the move: change the choice, change who exists.

cards.headline: Bad for whom?
cards.body: The trouble is a natural idea Parfit summed up as “what is bad must be bad for someone”. Combined with depletion, it implies the choice harms no one. Yet Parfit held that the great lowering of the quality of life must give some moral reason not to choose it. That clash is the non-identity problem.

cards.headline: Ways out
cards.body: Some philosophers, such as David Boonin, bite the bullet: such choices are not wrong after all. Others drop the idea that bad must be bad for someone and judge outcomes impersonally, as total utilitarianism does, by adding up well-being whoever has it. None of the replies has won the field; it remains among the most challenging problems in population ethics.

title: Could a Machine Matter Morally?
objective: After this level you can weigh what earlier theories of mind and morals imply about whether an artificial system could ever deserve moral concern.
summary: Whether an AI system could be a moral patient has no agreed answer in 2026; sentience, Kantian and relational views look for different evidence.

cards.headline: Could switching off a machine ever wrong the machine?
cards.body: Nobody has settled this. But the theories from this chapter tell you what would have to be true for the answer to be yes.

cards.headline: Agents and patients
cards.body: Philosophers split moral status in two. A moral agent has obligations; a moral patient is something moral agents have obligations toward. Humans are the typical agents, and sentient animals the typical patients. The standard view has been that AI systems have no moral status of any kind, but that view has come under pressure.

cards.headline: Bentham’s test, again
cards.body: Level 84’s question returns: can it suffer? In the moral status literature there is a trend toward seeing sentience as at least a necessary condition. That makes machine consciousness the hinge, and it worries some philosophers: Thomas Metzinger has called for a moratorium on synthetic phenomenology, research that risks creating artificial suffering.

cards.headline: Relations, not properties
cards.body: Mark Coeckelbergh and David Gunkel propose a relational turn. If we relate to robots as though they had rights, they argue, it may be futile to search for whether they really do. Joanna Bryson pushes from the other side: robots should not be given rights at all.

mascot.line: Keep this: the question is open. What you can do is say what each theory would need to see.

cards.headline: No verdict yet
cards.body: Line the views up and they look for different things. A sentience view asks whether the system can feel. A Kantian view asks for autonomy, the rational will Kant made the mark of beings whose interests count directly. A relational view looks at how we treat it. As of 2026 there is no agreed answer, and each view tells you what evidence would matter, not the verdict.

title: Is Beauty in the Eye of the Beholder?
objective: After this level you can weigh Hume's standard of taste against Kant's claim that a judgment of beauty speaks for everyone.
summary: Hume: beauty lives in feeling, but true critics’ joint verdict sets a standard. Kant: calling something beautiful claims everyone’s agreement. Each view faces an objection.

cards.headline: You love a song. Your friend can’t stand it. Is either of you wrong?
cards.body: Most people shrug: beauty is in the eye of the beholder. David Hume and Immanuel Kant weren’t satisfied with the shrug, and they disagreed about what should replace it.

cards.headline: Beauty lives in the feeling
cards.body: In “Of the Standard of Taste” (1757), Hume agreed that beauty is not a quality in objects: it belongs entirely to our feelings. Yet he refused to call every verdict equal. Rating the forgotten poet Ogilby as highly as Milton, he wrote, is like calling a molehill as high as a mountain, and we rightly call such taste absurd. So some feelings are better guides than others. The question is whose.

cards.headline: The key in the barrel
cards.body: Hume answers with a story. Two of Sancho’s kinsmen taste a barrel of wine. One praises it but detects a hint of leather; the other, a hint of iron. Everyone mocks them, until the barrel is emptied and an old key on a leather strap turns up at the bottom. True critics are like those tasters, Hume said: strong sense, delicate feeling, practice, comparison, no prejudice. Their joint verdict is the standard of taste.

mascot.line: People mix these up: “pleasant to me” is a report on you, while “beautiful” asks everyone to agree.

cards.headline: Kant: beauty speaks for everyone
cards.body: Kant, in his Critique of Judgment (1790), drew a sharper line. Call Canary wine pleasant and you should really say “pleasant to me”; nobody need argue. But call a poem beautiful and you judge “not merely for himself, but for every one”, with a universal voice. No rule or proof can force others to agree, yet you expect it. And the pleasure, Kant held, is disinterested: it involves no desire.

cards.headline: Each side’s weak spot
cards.body: Critics find a circle in Hume: great art is what true critics approve, but true critics are picked out by approving great art. Kant has critics too. Nietzsche attacked the idea that pleasure in beauty is free of desire, calling pleasure cut off from our passionate lives unrealistic. The debate is still open.

True critics’ joint verdict sets the standard
Kant: “beautiful” speaks for everyone
Each view faces a serious objection

title: What Makes Something Art?
objective: After this level you can compare three answers to "what is art?" (imitation, expression and the institutional theory) and apply them to an unusual case.
summary: Plato saw art as imitation, Tolstoy as passing on felt emotion, and Dickie as whatever the artworld presents for appreciation; each faces a standard objection.

cards.headline: Can a urinal be art?
cards.body: Marcel Duchamp presented one as an artwork called Fountain, and said he chose it for its lack of anything aesthetic. Whether he succeeded depends on what art is. Here are three answers.

cards.headline: Art as imitation
cards.body: The oldest answer: art imitates the world. Plato held that the arts are mimetic, and he ranked them low. A painted bed copies a real bed, which itself copies the Form. So a painting is only an appearance of an appearance. The theory suits a portrait. Its weak spot is music: a symphony doesn’t seem to imitate anything at all.

cards.headline: Art as expression
cards.body: Leo Tolstoy tried another answer. Art is one person handing on to others a feeling they have lived through, so that others are “infected” by it and feel it too. That explains why a sad song can leave you sad. Critics reply that a cheerful piece needn’t come from a cheerful composer: a sad one could have written it just as well.

cards.headline: Art by the artworld
cards.body: George Dickie’s institutional theory (1974) looks at the setting, not the object. A work of art is an artifact that someone acting for the artworld has put forward as a candidate for appreciation. Fountain passes easily. Critics call the theory circular: artworks, artists and the artworld are each defined by the others.

title: Epicurus on Fearing Death
objective: After this level you can explain Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us, and weigh the reply that death harms us by taking away future goods.
summary: Epicurus argued that death is nothing to us because good and bad need sensation; Lucretius compared the time after death to the time before birth; Nagel replied that death deprives us of life’s goods.

cards.headline: Should you fear something you will never experience?
cards.body: Epicurus thought the fear of death rests on a mistake, and he offered an argument to cure it. Philosophers have been testing that argument ever since.

cards.headline: Where death is, you are not
cards.body: In his Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus reasons in two steps. Good and bad require sensation, and death is the end of all sensation. So death is nothing to us, “seeing that, when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not.” Nothing can be bad for you if there is no you left to feel it.

cards.headline: The mirror behind you
cards.body: His follower Lucretius added a picture. Look back at the endless time before you were born. It never troubled you. Nature, he says, holds that time up like a mirror of the time after we are gone. If the first stretch of nothing holds nothing to fear, why fear the second?

cards.headline: What death takes away
cards.body: Thomas Nagel replied in his essay “Death” (1970). Something can be bad for you without being felt, if it takes away good things. Sleep through a celebration you’d longed for and you feel no pain, yet you lost something. Death, he argued, is bad in that way: it deprives you of the goods more life would have held.

title: The Stoic Split
objective: After this level you can explain the Stoic line between what is up to us and what is not, as Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius taught it, and apply it to a setback.
summary: Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius: only our views, aims and desires are up to us, and views, not things, disturb us. Aristotle replied that great misfortune can spoil a happy life.

cards.headline: Your train is cancelled. What, exactly, is up to you?
cards.body: Not the train. Epictetus, who spent part of his life enslaved before he was freed and opened his own school, built a way of living on sorting what is up to us from what is not.

cards.headline: Two piles
cards.body: His Handbook opens with the split. Within our power: opinion, aim, desire, aversion, in short our own doings. Beyond it: body, property, reputation, office. Treat the second pile as yours, Epictetus warned, and you will be hindered, you will lament, you will be disturbed. Keep to the first, and no one can compel you.

cards.headline: The view, not the thing
cards.body: Why does the split help? Because, Epictetus says, “men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.” The cancelled train is not up to you; your verdict that the day is ruined is. The emperor Marcus Aurelius, writing private notes to himself, put it bluntly: “Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged.”

cards.headline: Play hard, stay calm
cards.body: This isn’t giving up. Epictetus compared us to ball players who know the ball is worthless in itself, yet chase it with everything, because playing well is what matters. Use external things with care, he said, but with composure.

cards.headline: Aristotle draws the line elsewhere
cards.body: For Stoics like Marcus, happiness lies in virtue, which is wholly up to us. Aristotle disagreed. Happiness needs a complete life, he said, and no one calls a man happy who, like old King Priam, meets great misfortunes and dies wretched. For Aristotle, bad luck can reach into a good life.

title: The Experience Machine
objective: After this level you can use Robert Nozick's experience machine to weigh whether pleasure is all that makes a life go well.
summary: Nozick’s experience machine suggests something matters besides pleasant experience; De Brigard’s reversed case suggests the refusal may come from status quo bias.

cards.headline: Would you plug in for life?
cards.body: Picture a machine that gives you any experiences you want, and you’d never know you were in it. Robert Nozick bet you’d say no, and that your no reveals something about what makes a life go well.

cards.headline: The best offer ever made?
cards.body: Hedonists say pleasure is the only thing good for you in itself. In Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Nozick put that to the test. Imagine a machine that could give you any experiences you liked: writing a great novel, making a friend. Once plugged in, you couldn’t tell they weren’t real. If pleasure were all that mattered, plugging in for life would be the obvious choice.

cards.headline: What the machine leaves out
cards.body: Nozick thought plugging in would be a mistake. We want to do certain things, not just have the experience of doing them. We want to be a certain sort of person, not an indeterminate blob floating in a tank. And we want to make a real difference in the world. So, he concluded, something matters to us besides experience.

mascot.line: This is Level 3’s worry in action: imagined cases can mislead, so flip one and see if the answer holds.

cards.headline: Flip the machine
cards.body: Hedonists push back. In 2010 Felipe De Brigard reversed the case: suppose you learn you are already in a machine. Would you unplug into a reality you know nothing about? Many people chose to stay. Maybe the original no shows a preference for the familiar, the status quo bias, rather than a love of reality.

title: Nietzsche's Eternal Return
objective: After this level you can explain Nietzsche's test of living your life again forever and why he thought saying yes to it mattered after "God is dead".
summary: After diagnosing that “God is dead”, Nietzsche’s demon tests whether you can affirm this life as it is, forever. Readers dispute whether it is a test or a claim about time.

cards.headline: What if you had to live this exact life again, forever?
cards.body: Every joy and every pain, in the same order, with nothing new. Friedrich Nietzsche turned that nightmare, or dream, into a test.

cards.headline: “God is dead”
cards.body: In The Gay Science (1882), a madman announces that “God is dead”. He brings the news to people who already don’t believe, so Nietzsche’s point isn’t simply that atheism is true. It’s a diagnosis of a culture: belief in the Christian God had become unbelievable, so everything built on it, including Europe’s morality, was bound to collapse. What could give life value then?

cards.headline: The demon’s offer
cards.body: Near the end of the same book, a demon finds you in your loneliest loneliness. You must live this life again, innumerable times, “this spider and this moonlight among the trees” included. Would you gnash your teeth and curse him? Or answer, “Thou art a God, and never did I hear aught more divine!”? That question, Nietzsche wrote, would lie on every act as “the heaviest burden”.

cards.headline: Why the yes matters
cards.body: Many readers treat it as a thought experiment: your gut reaction shows how you really value your life, like being asked whether you’d marry your spouse again. On one reading it also blocks an escape. No later reward can redeem a life that returns forever, so the yes has to be to this life, as it is. Nietzsche’s name for that love was amor fati, love of fate.

cards.headline: Or a claim about time?
cards.body: Early readers took the return literally, as a theory that all events repeat in endless cycles, and critics raised problems for it read that way. Some scholars, such as Paul Loeb, still defend that reading. So even the idea’s basic status, test or theory, is contested.

The demon: live this life again, forever
The test asks for a yes to life as it is

title: Camus and the Absurd
objective: After this level you can explain Camus's absurd, the clash between our demand for meaning and a silent world, and why he pictured Sisyphus happy.
summary: For Camus the absurd is our longing for meaning meeting a silent world; he chose lucid revolt and pictured Sisyphus happy. Nagel suggested irony instead.

cards.headline: A boulder rolls back down. Forever. Could Sisyphus be happy?
cards.body: Albert Camus said yes. He meant it as an answer for everyone who has ever asked what it’s all for.

mascot.line: Keep this: for Camus the absurd is a relationship, you asking and the world staying silent, not a fact about either one.

cards.headline: Not a thing but a clash
cards.body: Camus opened The Myth of Sisyphus by calling one question fundamental: whether life is worth living. His diagnosis was the absurd. It isn’t in you, and it isn’t in the world. It’s the clash between them: your “wild longing for clarity” and the “unreasonable silence of the world”. You keep asking what it’s all for, and the universe doesn’t answer.

cards.headline: No escape hatches
cards.body: Camus refused every way out, from a leap toward hope in another life to giving up on this one. His answer was to go on living in revolt: clear-eyed, without false comfort, fully aware of life’s limits. Sisyphus, who knows his labor is hopeless and pushes on anyway, becomes the hero of the absurd.

cards.headline: Imagine him happy
cards.body: The book ends on its most famous lines: “The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.” The boulder never stays up. The pushing is the point.

cards.headline: Nagel: less drama, more irony
cards.body: Thomas Nagel doubted the heroics. In “The Absurd” (1971), he traced absurdity to our own ability to step back and see everything we take seriously as arbitrary. Defiance might make life nobler, he granted, but not less absurd. His suggested response was irony.

title: What Makes a Life Meaningful?
objective: After this level you can weigh views of meaning in life that locate it in God's purpose, in what you care about, or in Susan Wolf's mix of caring and real worth.
summary: Supernaturalists find meaning in God’s purpose, subjectivists in what you care about, and Susan Wolf in caring about what is truly worthwhile; each view faces a serious objection.

cards.headline: One person spends years curing a disease. Another builds a giant ball of string.
cards.body: Both love what they do. Are both lives equally meaningful? Philosophers give three main answers, and the ball of string is a famous test case.

cards.headline: Meaning from God’s purpose
cards.body: Supernaturalists hold that meaning needs a spiritual realm. Some, such as William Lane Craig, argue that only God’s purpose could ground the objective values a meaningful life needs. Critics, following Kurt Baier, reply that being created for a purpose would degrade us: we’d be expected to serve the aims of a superior being, a bit like a well-made tool.

cards.headline: Meaning from caring
cards.body: Subjectivists say meaning varies from person to person. For Harry Frankfurt, a life is meaningful to the extent that you care about or love something. That respects your own passions. The objection is the ball of string: critics such as Susan Wolf ask whether devotion to a pointless project could really make a life meaningful, however much it’s loved.

cards.headline: Wolf’s mix
cards.body: Wolf’s own view is a hybrid: “Meaning arises when subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness.” You have to care, and what you care about has to be truly worth caring about. Love something worthless, or do something worthwhile without caring, and no meaning accrues. Critics ask who decides what’s objectively worthwhile, and that question is still debated.

title: Thinking Like a Philosopher
objective: After this level you can take a new big question through the tree's toolkit: clarify the terms, test it with a thought experiment, and weigh the rival views.
summary: “Would it be good to live forever?” through the toolkit: clarify it, test it with Williams’s Makropulos case, and weigh his tedium argument against the replies.

cards.headline: Would it be good to live forever?
cards.body: Here’s a big question this tree hasn’t answered. Rather than hand you a verdict, this level takes it through the toolkit: clarify it, test it, weigh the rivals.

cards.headline: Step 1: pin down the question
cards.body: “Forever” could mean endless old age, which is not the interesting question. So philosophers sharpen it: suppose you stayed healthy and mentally sharp, indefinitely. Bernard Williams added two conditions for wanting such a life: it should clearly be you who lives forever, and that life should connect to the aims you have now.

cards.headline: Step 2: build a case
cards.body: In “The Makropulos Case” (1973), Williams borrowed a character from a play by Karel Čapek. Elina Makropulos took an elixir of life; at 342, she has reached a state of boredom and indifference. Williams argued that, given enough time, the deep desires that make us want a future would run out, and boredom would set in.

cards.headline: Step 3: weigh the rivals
cards.body: Nagel, Jonathan Glover and John Martin Fischer replied that an endless life needn’t grow dull: your interests could keep changing. Williams answered that swapping in new desires and a new character makes it unclear the later person is still you, breaking his first condition. The question remains controversial, and now you know how to join it.
